posts.title: aluminum composite shell and bamboo interior define lavvu mobile home unit in armenia
posts.description: AUTOMOTIVE-INSPIRED STEEL FRAME STRUCTURES FACTORY-BUILT MODULE Developed and manufactured in Armenia by Re:Büro, LAVVU XL is a transportable modular dwelling that applies automotive manufacturing principles to residential architecture. Rather than relying on conventional on-site construction, each unit is fabricated under controlled factory conditions as a single self-contained volume integrating structure, interior finishes, furniture, and building systems. At the core of the module is a welded steel frame paired with lightweight internal framing, mineral wool insulation, and an aluminum composite exterior shell. all images ©Re:Büro PANORAMIC DOORS AND SEMICIRCULAR WINDOW FRAME outdoor VIEWS Encompassing approximately 22 sqm, the LAVVU XL model by studio Re:Büro opens its compact footprint to the outdoors through triple-glazed panoramic folding glass doors, rooflights, and a semicircular end window. posts.title: 1960s grand touring car design shapes acte deux’s paris apartment renovation
posts.description: acte deux reimagines 1960s paris apartment through car design Acte Deux , founded by Johanna Lapray and Hugo L’ahélec, renovates a 65-square-meter apartment in the Paris ’s 18th arrondissement, drawing on the streamlined forms and richly appointed interiors of 1960s grand touring cars . Named Gran Turismo, the project takes its reference from an era of automotive design associated with sculptural bodywork, polished details and comfortable interiors, translating these qualities into a domestic setting. Located on the 10th floor of a 1960s concrete residential building, the apartment originally had standard ceiling heights and relatively constrained volumes. posts.title: sinuous stone-roofed visitor center meanders through the mountains of china
posts.description: winding stone roofs follow the movement of water in guizhou The Huangguoshu Scenic Area in China ‘s mountainous Guizhou province welcomes visitors beneath a pair of serpentine roofs designed by the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design (CAUPD) and AEPA&TSC. The two Beijing-based practices take their formal cues from the movement of the Baishui River, which runs through the region and feeds a waterfall. The project comprises two visitor centers at the entrances to the Great Waterfall and Tianxingqiao scenic areas. From above, the architecture appears as a series of dark, sinuous ribbons among densely forested mountains. Much of the enclosed building volume disappears beneath grassy slopes, while the extended rooflines trace the paths of visitors through the landscape. The project grew out of a need to accommodate increasing numbers of tourists in an area whose entrance facilities had become overwhelmed.
